analysis.one_liner: Creates a universal public health plan funded by payroll taxes, a tax on millionaires, and a securities-trading tax.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it was referred to five House committees, then to subcommittees, where it sat with zero cosponsors until the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced private health insurance with a state-run program guaranteeing every U.S. resident comprehensive coverage — hospital care, doctors, prescription drugs, dental, vision, mental health, and long-term care — with no charges at the point of care. It would have ended Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, federal employee coverage, and TRICARE as they existed, and repealed the Affordable Care Act's coverage rules. To pay for it, it would have imposed a payroll tax on employers, a new health care income tax, a surcharge on incomes over $1 million, and a tax on securities trades. It was never considered.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. citizen, national, and lawful resident — including the uninsured, people who are underinsured, and anyone paying premiums or facing deductibles. Everyone would get automatic enrollment, a health security card, and coverage without copays, deductibles, or balance billing, including services many private plans limit or exclude: dental, eyeglasses and hearing aids, prescription drugs, mental health and substance abuse treatment, and home and community-based long-term care. Benefits would be portable between states and could not be sold back to private insurers as duplicate coverage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Every U.S. resident needing health care

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. citizen, national, and lawful resident would be entitled to health care benefits through their state's health security program, with automatic enrollment at birth or immigration

Covered services would include hospital care, professional services, prescription drugs, dental care, mental health and substance abuse treatment, preventive services including eyeglasses and hearing aids, and home and community-based long-term care
No person could impose any charge for covered services — no copays, deductibles, or balance billing — and states would have to prohibit the sale of insurance duplicating program benefits
Benefits would be portable across states, with a maximum waiting period of 3 months for new residents and payment for care received while temporarily out of state

analysis.who_pays: Employers through a new payroll tax; individuals through a new health care income tax; households with modified adjusted gross income over $1 million through an income surcharge; and investors through an excise tax on securities transactions. Health insurers would lose the market for core coverage, since states must bar sale of plans duplicating program benefits, and existing programs — Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, federal employee coverage, and TRICARE — would be wound down into the new system.

drawbacks.text: The bill funds universal coverage with substantial new taxes: a payroll tax on employers, a health care income tax on individuals, a surcharge on incomes over $1 million, and an excise tax on securities transactions

It would end Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and TRICARE for services after December 31, 2014 — requiring tens of millions of people to move into an untested new program at a single date, with only narrow transition rules for in-progress hospital stays

States must prohibit the sale of health insurance that duplicates program benefits, eliminating the option of buying private core coverage and narrowing consumer choice, though employers and unions could still offer supplemental benefits
Coverage has real limits: inpatient mental health care is capped at roughly 60 days a year, and non-emergency dental treatment for adults is not covered until 2020

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was the broadest version of the recurring single-payer proposal: everyone covered, no cost-sharing, dedicated funding, and a ban on duplicate private insurance that would make the public program the main channel for care. The trade-offs were real and were written into the bill — large new taxes, a one-date transition that would have swept everyone out of Medicare, Medicaid, employer plans, and TRICARE simultaneously, and capped benefits in areas like adult dental care and inpatient mental health. Whether the state-based structure could have held budgets and quality across 50 states was never tested, because the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to five House committees in March 2013 and sent to subcommittees, none of which ever held a hearing or a vote, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott introduced the American Health Security Act of 2013 on March 14, 2013

The bill was referred to five committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Oversight and Government Reform, Armed Services, and Education and the Workforce — and then to subcommittees, including the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health
No hearing, markup, or vote was ever held on the bill in any committee or on the House floor
The bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The health insurance industry and the existing coverage system came out ahead: because the bill never advanced, private insurers kept the core coverage market, employers kept their current benefit structures, and the Affordable Care Act's private-insurance framework stayed in place. No one who would have paid the new payroll, income, surcharge, or securities taxes ever paid them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and the status quo

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded, so no roll-call exists; the sole sponsor was a Democrat, the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, and every committee it sat in was chaired by a Republican in the Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: The bill would have repealed the Affordable Care Act's coverage framework, eliminated Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and federal employee private coverage, and barred states from allowing sale of insurance duplicating the public program's benefits — removing the core private health insurance market. Insurers' interest in keeping that market ran directly against the bill's promise of universal no-charge coverage.

An excise tax on securities transactions would have been imposed to fund the program, and traders could have claimed an income tax credit for it. The industry's cost of the tax is the funding source for universal coverage.

Providers would have received guaranteed payment through state-set global budgets for hospitals and fee schedules for practitioners, ending unpaid care, but at rates capped by a national health budget. Providers would gain a universal payer yet lose the ability to bill insurers and patients above program rates.

Prescription drugs would have been a covered benefit for everyone, enlarging the customer base, but payment would have been set under state fee schedules rather than negotiated with private insurers. Universal access cuts against the industry's ability to price above program rates.

Employers would have paid a new payroll tax but shed the cost and administration of core health coverage, which ERISA-based group plans could no longer duplicate. Their existing benefit arrangements would have been dismantled even as their tax bill rose.

An income tax surcharge on modified adjusted gross income above $1 million would have helped finance the program. The households bearing it are those whose current out-of-pocket exposure to health costs is lowest relative to income.
